name: Each-uisge
description: A shapeshifting Celtic water horse of Scottish and Irish folklore, considered the fiercest of all water horses; lures riders into sea lochs and freshwater lochs and devours all but their livers.
full_description: The each-uisge ([ɛxˈɯʃkʲə], 'water horse') is a malevolent water spirit of Scottish Highland folklore, with a close Irish cognate (each-uisce / aughisky) and Manx cognate (cabyll-ushtey). Folklorist Katharine Briggs called it 'perhaps the fiercest and most dangerous of all the water-horses'. It is a shapeshifter, appearing most often as a fine horse or pony but also as a handsome young man or, in some accounts, an enormous bird. When mounted in horse form, the rider is initially safe; once the creature reaches water, its skin turns adhesive and it plunges to the deepest part of the loch, drowning the rider and devouring the body — except, traditionally, the liver, which floats ashore and identifies the cause of death. Unlike the kelpie, which haunts streams and rivers, the each-uisge frequents sea lochs and large freshwater lochs of the Highlands and Hebrides. The creature is documented in 19th-century collections by John Gregorson Campbell and J. F. Campbell, and synthesised in modern scholarship by Katharine Briggs.
origin: Folkloric range across the Scottish Highlands and Hebrides, with cognates in Ireland (each-uisce / aughisky) and the Isle of Man (cabyll-ushtey).

etymology.origin: Scottish Gaelic 'each' (horse) + 'uisge' (water); cognates each-uisce in Irish and cabyll-ushtey in Manx (cabbyl 'horse' + ushtey 'water').
etymology.first_use: Recorded throughout 19th-century Scottish Gaelic folklore collections.

timeline.event: John Francis Campbell publishes 'Popular Tales of the West Highlands', containing several each-uisge tales
timeline.significance: First major scholarly documentation in English

timeline.event: John Gregorson Campbell publishes 'Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland', with a chapter on water-horses
timeline.significance: Classic ethnographic treatment of the each-uisge

timeline.event: Katharine Briggs publishes 'A Dictionary of Fairies', characterising the each-uisge as 'perhaps the fiercest and most dangerous of all the water-horses'

cultural_notes: Anyone who mounts an each-uisge near water is doomed; the liver floating ashore is the only sign of the victim's fate. Folk practice held that a horse encountered alone near a loch should never be ridden or even touched.
